China Electric Truck Export Checklist: Route, Payload, Charging and Compliance

The information an international buyer should freeze before quotation, production, shipment and local acceptance.

BUYER GUIDESeptember 23, 20269 min read
ChecklistRouteVehicleChargingComplianceShipping

Start with the job, not a model photo. A reliable quotation needs country, application, payload or GCW, daily route, grade, climate, body or trailer, charging standard, local approval pathway, quantity and delivery expectations.

1. Document the duty cycle

Record loaded, partial and empty kilometres; maximum and average payload; road grade; surface; speed; stops; queues; shifts and operating days. Add ambient temperature, rain, dust, mud and altitude where relevant. For tractors include trailer type and GCW. For dump trucks include material density, body volume and cycles. For refrigerated cargo include temperature, door openings and auxiliary power.

Ask the supplier to match battery, motor, axle layout and charging to this route. Do not treat catalogue battery capacity as a guaranteed range. Define an operating reserve for detours, congestion and charger unavailability.

2. Freeze the completed vehicle

Confirm left- or right-hand drive, axle layout, GVW or GCW, wheelbase, tyres, suspension, braking systems, cab and safety equipment. Specify body dimensions, material, doors, tail lift, refrigeration, tipping system or fifth wheel. Request an axle-load and completed-vehicle mass calculation before body fabrication.

List every interface: trailer connections, body power, PTO or auxiliary drive, charging inlet, telematics and diagnostic access. Identify which party supplies and warrants the chassis, body and auxiliary equipment. Review the relevant tractor, cargo and dump ranges.

3. Match charging before production

State the destination connector and communication standard, site voltage, transformer capacity, charger model, available current, number of bays and charging window. GB and EU interfaces appear on different catalogue configurations and must not be assumed interchangeable. Put the approved inlet and charger compatibility in the signed specification.

Model simultaneous demand when several trucks return together. Include grid upgrades, switchgear, cables, civil work, commissioning, charger service and redundancy. Agree how a truck is recovered if its normal charger is unavailable.

4. Confirm the local approval pathway

Right-hand drive or an EU charging interface does not itself guarantee registration. The importer should confirm current dimensional, axle-load, braking, lighting, visibility, high-voltage, electromagnetic and driver-assistance requirements with the destination authority or qualified local specialist. State whether operation is on public roads or a closed industrial site.

Agree who is responsible for chassis evidence, body approval and completed-vehicle inspection. Freeze approved drawings, permitted substitutions and change control. A late component change may affect mass, charging compatibility or documentation.

5. Prepare documents, logistics and acceptance

Agree the required commercial invoice, packing list, transport document, identification records, available conformity evidence, battery shipping information, manuals and parts documents. The exact file depends on the market and shipment. Confirm port, dimensions, lashing, transport state of charge, handling and receiving inspection with the logistics provider.

Before dispatch, compare the completed truck with the signed specification. Check identification, steering side, lights, labels, charging inlet, supplied cables, body dimensions, tyres and document numbers. Photograph the inspection and record open items.

6. Build after-sales readiness

Define warranty documents, service schedule, diagnostic method, high-voltage training, remote support and parts stocking. Prepare routine filters, brake and suspension items, charging components and body-specific parts according to fleet size and lead time. Confirm who handles technical escalation after arrival.

7. Assign responsibility in writing

An export project often includes a chassis supplier, body builder, charger supplier, shipping company, importer and local service partner. Record which party owns every deliverable and decision. The responsibility matrix should cover technical drawings, body integration, axle-load calculation, charging compatibility, homologation evidence, battery transport documents, export clearance, destination clearance, commissioning, driver training and warranty support.

Define the document language, approval deadline and sign-off authority. If a local importer must obtain permits or registration, place that requirement in the project schedule before production. If the body is installed after arrival, confirm chassis interfaces, allowable loads, electrical demand and warranty boundaries before shipment. Written ownership reduces delays caused by assumptions between suppliers.

8. Control changes after technical approval

Once the buyer approves the configuration, create a controlled specification with model code, steering side, axle layout, battery capacity, motor, tyres, cab equipment, safety systems, charging inlet, body interfaces and supplied accessories. Drawings and commercial documents should reference the same revision. Any proposed substitution should identify the reason and its effect on compatibility, mass, performance, compliance, delivery and price.

Do not accept a verbal statement that a replacement part is equivalent. Ask for the updated specification and evidence needed by the destination market. Recalculate completed-vehicle mass and axle loads when the body, battery, spare wheel, auxiliary equipment or chassis component changes. Confirm connector and communication compatibility again if charging hardware changes.

9. Plan factory and destination acceptance

Prepare an acceptance checklist before production finishes. At the factory, verify identification, visible configuration, steering position, tyre specification, charging inlet, lights, cab equipment, body dimensions, supplied tools and diagnostic items. Where contractually agreed, record charging communication, basic function tests and warning-free startup. Match serial numbers and document references, then retain dated photographs.

Repeat a receiving inspection after transport. Check for shipping damage, fluid leaks, loose accessories, battery and 24-volt state, tyre condition and document completeness before the vehicle enters service. Commission the approved charger, train operators on shutdown and emergency procedures, and keep the vehicle within the documented operating limits during initial route validation. Acceptance records provide a clear starting point for warranty and service discussions.

Agree in advance what constitutes a minor open item, a condition that delays shipment and a condition that prevents acceptance. Define the time allowed for correction and the evidence required to close each item. The buyer should receive the final approved specification and acceptance record in a durable project file rather than relying on chat messages or photographs without model and serial references.

10. Prepare the first operating month

Before the truck enters revenue service, assign routes that fit the approved configuration and charging plan. Record driver, payload, distance, start and return SOC, charging energy, charging time and any warning. Use the same route and load definitions established during procurement so early operating data can be compared with the project assumptions.

Schedule an early technical review with the supplier or service partner. Confirm tyre pressures, fastener and fluid checks, body operation, charging events and driver feedback according to the delivered maintenance information. Keep spare keys, emergency contacts, manuals and high-voltage procedures accessible to the operating team. A disciplined first month catches integration and training issues before they become recurring downtime.

11. Evaluate the supplier response, not only the price

A useful supplier should ask questions about the duty cycle, completed body, destination approval and charging site before confirming a model. Compare quotations line by line: exact configuration, inclusions, exclusions, documentation, production assumptions, delivery terms, warranty, commissioning and support. A lower price with an undefined charging interface or body responsibility can create a larger project risk than a clearly specified proposal.

Request one controlled technical and commercial document set. Confirm how questions and changes are approved, which language governs the specification and who can make binding commitments. This gives procurement, engineering, logistics and finance the same reference and makes competing proposals easier to compare fairly.

Information to send with an enquiry

  • Country, port, quantity and target delivery.
  • Application, payload, GVW or GCW and body or trailer.
  • Daily distance, grade, surface, shifts and climate.
  • Drive side, charging standard and site power.
  • Public-road or closed-site use and approval pathway.
  • Required documents, inspection and spare-parts plan.

Frequently asked questions

Can a quotation be based only on payload?

No. Route, body, grade, charging, climate and legal limits also affect selection.

Does an EU connector guarantee market approval?

No. Charging compatibility and vehicle homologation are separate checks.

Who should confirm regulations?

The importer should verify current requirements with the destination authority or qualified compliance partner.
